extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, physicists, and advanced students studying Newtonian classical mechanics (readers of Newton's Principia); historians of science
extracted.subtask_description: A sequence of propositions, lemmas, corollaries, examples and rules from Newton's Principia (Latin) treating motion in resisting media, laws of resistance (esp. proportional to velocity^2), infinitesimal moments, and how medium density must vary for motion on prescribed curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V (Theor. III): behavior under resistance ∝ velocity^2
rubrics_metrics.description: _Si corpori resistitur in velocitatis ratione duplicata, & sola vi insita per Medium similare movetur, tempora vero sumantur in progressione Geometrica a minoribus terminis ad majores pergente: dico quod velocitates initio singulorum temporum sunt in eadem progressione Geometrica inverse, & quod spatia sunt æqualia quæ singulis temporibus describuntur._
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: If resistance ∝ square of velocity, and decrement of velocity ∝ resistance, then dividing time into equal infinitesimal parts the squares of velocities at each part are proportional to the differences of velocities; hence the sequence of squares (and thus velocities) follows an inverse geometric progression when times are taken in geometric progression. Corollaries: (1) If total time is represented by an asymptote segment AD and initial velocity by ordinate AB, final velocity corresponds to ordinate DG and total space by adjacent hyperbolic area ABGD; (2) ratio of space in resisting medium to space with uniform velocity equals area ABGD to rectangle AB×AD; (3–5) relations giving time and point on the hyperbola when resistance is compared to a given centripetal force. Use/implication: gives the general geometric relation of velocities, times and spaces when medium resistance is quadratic in velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VI (Theor. IV): equal spheres in medium with resistance ∝ velocity^2
rubrics_metrics.description: _Corpora Sphærica homogenea & æqualia, resistentiis in duplicata ratione velocitatum impedita, & solis viribus insitis incitata, temporibus quæ sunt reciproce ut velocitates sub initio, describunt semper æqualia spatia, & amittunt partes velocitatum proportionales totis._
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If homogeneous equal spheres moving under their own impressed forces in a medium whose resistance ∝ v^2, then times which are reciprocals of initial velocities correspond to equal distances described, and the parts of velocity lost are proportional to the total velocities. The argument uses hyperbolic areas and similar triangles to show equal areas (spaces) and proportional loss of motion. (This proposition establishes how equal bodies under quadratic resistance experience loss of motion proportionally and traverse equal distances in matched time intervals.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VII (Theor. V): relation of time, resistance, and loss of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: _Corpora Sphærica quibus resistitur in duplicata ratione velocitatum, temporibus quæ sunt ut motus primi directe & resistentiæ primæ inverse, amittent partes motuum proportionales totis, & spatia describent temporibus istis in velocitates primas ductis proportionalia._
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement: For spheres resisted as v^2, if times are as initial motion directly and as the initial resistance inversely, they lose parts of motion proportional to the whole and describe spaces proportional to (initial velocity × time). Explanation: the lost parts of motion are proportional to resistance × time; to make those parts proportional to the whole, time must scale as motion directly and resistance inversely. Consequence: with given initial velocity ratios, they always describe spaces proportional to initial velocities multiplied by time. (Gives a scaling rule linking time, resistance and retained motion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma II: rule for moments (infinitesimal increments) of generated quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: _Momentum Genitæ æquatur momentis Terminorum singulorum generantium in eorundem laterum indices dignitatum & coefficientia continue ductis._
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma gives the standard rules for 'moments' (infinitesimal increments) of algebraic and geometric expressions: e.g., moment of product AB is aB + Ab; of ABC is ABc + AbC + aBC; of A^n is n a A^{n-1}; of 1/A is -a/A^2; and general rule for A^{m/n} and for products/quotients with integer or fractional, positive or negative exponents. Cases and corollaries expand to continuous proportionals, four proportionals, and sums/differences of squares. Scholium: Newton notes Leibniz communicated a similar method; lemma underlies methods for maxima/minima, tangents, etc. Use: fundamental infinitesimal algebraic differentiation rules for handling varying quantities and deriving differentials in propositions that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII (Theor. VI): geometric progression of absolute forces in uniform medium under gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: _Si corpus in Medio uniformi, Gravitate uniformiter agente, recta ascendat vel descendat, & spatium totum descriptum distinguatur in partes æquales, inq; principiis singularum partium (addendo resistentiam Medii ad vim gravitatis, quando corpus ascendit, vel subducendo ipsam quando corpus descendit) colligantur vires absolutæ; dico quod vires illæ absolutæ sunt in progressione Geometrica._
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement and proof: Represent gravity by a given line AC and resistance by AK; the absolute force at each segment (gravity ± resistance) corresponds to ordinates of a hyperbola. Dividing total area into equal parts shows the absolute forces form a geometric progression. Corollaries: (1) one can represent gravity, velocity and resistance by respective lines if total space is a hyperbolic area; (2) the maximum velocity obtainable by infinite descent equals line AC; (3–5) methods to find maximum velocity from known resistance at some speed and relations for infinitesimal time particles as rectangles KN×PQ and PQ/CK. Use: connects hyperbolic geometrical constructions with velocities, resistances and times for bodies in uniform resisting media under gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IX (Theor. VII): sector areas correspond to ascent/descent times
rubrics_metrics.description: _Positis jam demonstratis, dico quod si Tangentes angulorum sectoris Circularis & sectoris Hyperbolici sumantur velocitatibus proportionales, existente radio justæ magnitudinis: erit tempus omne ascensus futuri ut sector Circuli, & tempus omne descensus præteriti ut sector Hyperbolæ._
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the tangents of angles of circular and hyperbolic sectors are taken proportional to velocities (with a suitable radius), then the total future ascent time is proportional to the circular sector area and the total past descent time to the hyperbolic sector area. Proof decomposes sectors into infinitesimal particles and matches those to infinitesimal time particles related to changes in velocity. Corollaries: relations comparing spaces in resisting vs. non-resisting media via areas (sector hyperbolic vs. triangle), formulae linking instantaneous velocities in resisting vs. non-resisting media (triangles vs. sectors), and methods to get time and space given areas. Use: a geometric method to map sector areas to physical times and spaces under resistance laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X (Prob. III): determining medium density and velocity field to produce motion on a prescribed curve
rubrics_metrics.description: _Tendat uniformis vis gravitatis directe ad planum Horizontis, sitq; resistentia ut medii densitas & quadratum velocitatis conjunctim: requiritur tum Medii densitas in locis singulis, quæ faciat ut corpus in data quavis linea curva moveatur, tum corporis velocitas in iisdem locis._
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: Given gravity acting uniformly towards horizontal plane and resistance ∝ (medium density) × (v^2), find the medium density distribution and the body's velocity at each point so that the body moves along a given curve. Method: relate infinitesimal displacements due to gravity and resistance, use Lemma I and series expansions to resolve perpendiculars and tangents. Examples provided: (1) semicircle — deduce medium density ∝ length of tangent CT (so that projectile follows a circle quadrant); (2) parabola — no finite medium density will produce motion in parabola (recovering Galileo); (3) hyperbola — compute density series to make projectile move on a given hyperbola; (4) general hyperbola law with VG ∝ 1/DN^n leads to density formula via series expansion. Guidance includes explicit series-expansion techniques, identification of terms representing tangent, curvature, variation of curvature, and practical truncation: initial terms determine tangent and curvature; higher terms give finer corrections. Scholium: motion in parabola occurs only in non-resistant media, whereas hyperbolic trajectories arise from persistent resistance; curves in realistic media approximate these hyperbolas. Use: gives constructive rules to design medium-density profiles to force a projectile to follow a prescribed curve, using expansions and matching coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium on curves and applicability: hyperbolic-type curves approximate real trajectories in resisting media
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion: Since motion in parabola occurs only in non-resistant media, and in the described hyperbolas arises through continual resistance, the actual curve a projectile describes in a uniformly resisting medium is closer to these hyperbolas than to a parabola. The actual curve is of hyperbolic kind but with vertex region differing from the ideal hyperbolas described; in remote parts it approaches asymptotes more closely. These practical hyperbolas may be more useful than more exact but more complicated hyperbolas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: when modeling projectile motion in resisting media, prefer hyperbolic-type approximations with series expansion corrections near the vertex for practical calculations. The text explains constructing tangent-based approximations and using reciprocal tangents to infer density and resistance at points; it recommends truncating series when higher terms become negligible for application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulae (Reg. 1–3): practical relations among medium density, angle, velocity and resistance
rubrics_metrics.description:
Reg. 1: _Si servetur Medii densitas in A & mutetur angulus NAH, manebunt longitudines AH, AI, HX. Ideoq; si longitudines illæ in aliquo casu inveniantur, Hyperbola deinceps ex dato quovis angulo NAH expedite determinari potest._

Reg. 2: _Si servetur tum angulus NAH tum Medii densitas in A, & mutetur velocitas quacum corpus projicitur; servabitur longitudo AH, & mutabitur AI in duplicata ratione velocitatis reciproce._

Reg. 3: (continued) If both angle NAH and the body's speed in A and the accelerating gravity are held, and the proportion of resistance in A to the moving gravity is increased in any ratio: the ratio AH to AI will increase by the same ratio, with the parabola's latus rectum proportional to AH^2/AI; hence AH decreases by that ratio and AI decreases in the doubled ratio. Also comments on how resistance to weight changes when specific gravity or medium density change, and when resistance scales differently with size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three practical rules summarize how preserving or changing any two of (local medium density, projection angle, initial velocity, gravity) determines the geometric lengths AH, AI (which determine the hyperbola/asymptotes) and thus the resulting trajectory. They provide rapid methods to adjust parameters: e.g., keep density fixed and change angle to maintain certain distances; keep angle and density fixed and vary speed—AI scales inversely with square of velocity, etc. Reg.3 discusses how increasing resistance-to-weight ratio affects AH and AI and thus the shape, and notes effects when specimen density or medium density vary. Use: ready heuristics for designing or predicting projectile trajectories in media with variable density.
